title: Images
hookLine: Orthodox honor icons; Catholics statues; Reformed churches keep walls plain from the second commandment

cards: The walls of an Orthodox church look back at you. Christ, Mary, apostles and saints, painted in gold and deep color, face you from the walls and the screen before the altar.
People coming in kiss the icons and light candles in front of them. Now step into a Reformed church: white walls, clear windows, a pulpit, a table, an open Bible, and very little else.
Both rooms are built for prayer to the same God. Both were made to look that way on purpose.

teach.b: Start with the commandment. In Exodus, God says: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above." And the next verse: don't bow down to them.
Reformed churches count this as the second commandment, and they take it seriously: no images in worship, so nothing stands between the worshiper and the living God, met in his word.
For them, plain walls are a form of reverence.
But later in the same book, God tells Moses to make two cherubim of beaten gold for the cover of the ark. So images were not simply absent from Israel's worship. The Orthodox build on another verse.

teach.h: THE IMAGE OF THE INVISIBLE GOD.
teach.b: Paul calls Christ "the image of the invisible God." Their argument, made by John of Damascus when icons were under attack: the invisible God can't be painted.

But when God became human, he could be seen and touched, and what can be seen can be pictured. So icons are honored, kissed and prayed before. The honor, they say, passes to the one shown; worship belongs to God alone.
Catholics keep statues and paintings, crucifixes and stained glass, in a similar spirit: a picture as a way in, never the thing worshiped.
Other Protestant churches sit in between, with a plain cross, a window, or a painting of the Last Supper. So the argument isn't really whether images are good or bad.
Each church is guarding something: the commandment, or the God who became visible. And each is asking what helps people pray, and what gets in the way.

how: Orthodox Christians venerate icons at home and in church, often kissing them and lighting candles before them; Catholic churches hold statues, crucifixes and stained glass; Reformed churches keep their worship spaces plain.

o: the pictures a prophet sees in a vision
the symbols carved on the outside of a church
icons, statues and pictures in places of prayer

games.q: what each church guards — tap the pairs.
p: the image of the invisible God

s: Israel's worship in Exodus had no images at all
God tells Moses to make two cherubim of beaten gold for the ark.
the Orthodox say icons are worshiped as God
they honor icons; the honor passes to the one shown, and worship belongs to God alone.
Reformed churches keep their walls plain on purpose
to guard the commandment against graven images in worship.

games.q: you're defending icons. someone objects: God is invisible, so no one may picture him. how does John of Damascus answer?
o: when God became human, he could be seen, and so pictured.
games.why: the invisible God can't be painted, but God made visible in Christ can. that's the heart of the case for icons.

practice: Let your eyes move slowly around the place where you pray, or where you go to be quiet: a cross, a candle, a photo, a window, a blank wall, or nothing at all.

Ask of each thing: does this help me be still, or pull me somewhere else? Just notice, without changing anything; if you pray, ask God for whatever helps, and if you don't, let the looking be the practice.

wordCard.voice: Images. Icons, statues and pictures: honored by some churches as windows toward God, kept out by others to guard the commandment.

orig.note: Greek: image. Paul uses it for Christ in Colossians 1:15, "the image of the invisible God."

carryVoice: Your line: what helps you pray. Gold walls and white ones, both on purpose. See you next time.
